extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, attorneys, agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification and original disclosure satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112, first paragraph) and related provisions, including support for amended/new claims and entitlement to earlier priority dates. Focuses on when disclosure shows inventor was in possession of the claimed invention (species and genus analyses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description is a factual, case-by-case inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description 'inquiry is a factual one and must be assessed on a case-by-case basis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite precedent (Faulding, Pfaff) and treat determination as fact-specific rather than amenable to bright-line rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual reduction to practice evidences completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification may describe an actual reduction to practice by showing that the inventor constructed an embodiment or performed a process that met all the limitations of the claim and determined that the invention would work for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Cooper v. Goldfarb; UMC Elecs.; Estee Lauder v. L'Oreal; Mahurkar — reduction to physical embodiment including all claim limitations is required for reduction to practice; for biological materials, a deposit per 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. (esp. 1.804, 1.809) can demonstrate an actual reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings or structural chemical formulas can show possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed can show inventor was in possession of the claimed invention as a whole (drawings alone may provide a 'written description').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vas-Cath; In re Wolfensperger; Autogiro. In chemical claims, generic formulae usually indicate what the generic claims encompass (Eli Lilly). Use drawings where visual representation can 'flesh out' words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description need only cover what is new or non-conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: The description need only describe in detail that which is new or not conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Hybritech principle: do not require disclosure of conventional aspects in detail; focus on the inventive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying characteristics may demonstrate possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of sufficiently detailed, relevant identifying characteristics (complete or partial structure, other physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics with a known/disclosed correlation between function and structure, or combinations thereof) may show possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with structure-function correlation, and method of making. Cases: Enzo Biochem; Written Description Guidelines. In biotech, sequence, structure, binding affinity/specificity, molecular weight, length are examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-only descriptions are generally insufficient for compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing a composition by its function alone typically will not suffice to sufficiently describe the composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eli Lilly and Fiers: a gene or chemical defined only by function does not reveal 'what it is.' Adequate written description of a chemical invention requires a precise definition by structure, formula, chemical name, or physical properties, not merely a wish or plan for obtaining it. Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle example: method-of-use without compounds disclosed was insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) support requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph), the corresponding structure, materials, or acts must be described in the specification and interpreted to cover their equivalents; written description must adequately link described structure/materials/acts to the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must consider original disclosure across summary, detailed description, claims, abstract, and drawings. Two adequate-description paths: (1) written description adequately links particular structure/materials/acts to perform function, or (2) clear from facts that skilled artisan would know what structure/materials/acts perform the function (Aristocrat; Atmel; Biomedino). If insufficient corresponding structure -> rejection under 112(b)/(second paragraph) and also 112(a)/(first paragraph). See MPEP §2181 and related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional or well-known matter need not be disclosed in detail
rubrics_metrics.description: What is conventional or well known to one of ordinary skill in the art need not be disclosed in detail in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply in context of the art's maturity (Hybritech; Capon): balance between known material and inventor's contribution evolves with the field; in mature fields less disclosure of known techniques may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different analysis for claims to a single species vs a genus
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limited to a single disclosed embodiment/species is analyzed as a species claim; a claim encompassing two or more embodiments/species is analyzed as a genus claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §806.04(e). The written description showing required differs for species vs genus (see subsequent specific steps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Species claim evaluation steps (i)(A)-(C)
rubrics_metrics.description: (A) Determine whether application describes an actual reduction to practice of the claimed invention. (B) If not, determine whether invention is complete as evidenced by reduction to drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed. (C) If not, determine whether specification sets forth distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficiently detailed to show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If complete structure disclosed -> written description satisfied for that species and rejection should not be made. If not, evaluate other identifying characteristics and whether disclosure is 'in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms' to show possession (35 U.S.C. 112(a)). Cases: Fields v. Conover; In re Wilder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether complete structure or acts are disclosed for species
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the application as filed describes the complete structure (or acts of a process) of the claimed invention as a whole; a complete structure typically satisfies the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete structural disclosure meets 35 U.S.C. 112(a). If not disclosed, look for other identifying characteristics (see i(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of structure-function correlation when direct structure not disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: In biotechnology, if a strong correlation between structure and function is established, one skilled in the art may predict structure from recited function; written description may be satisfied through disclosure of function and minimal structure when there is a well-established correlation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enzo Biochem and Written Description Guidelines: where such correlation exists, functional recitation + minimal structure can suffice; where it does not, function-only disclosure is likely a 'wish' and inadequate (Eli Lilly; In re Wilder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in possession determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the specification shows that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention is a factual determination reached by considering a number of factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics (with correlation), and method of making. Also consider state of knowledge, maturity of art, and pertinent prior patents/printed publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpredictable arts require more evidence to show possession
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions in unpredictable arts or emerging technologies, more evidence is required to show possession; disclosure of method+function may not be sufficient to support product-by-process claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Amgen, Fiers — conception not achieved for complex genes until reduction to practice/actual isolation; disclosure that fails to enable recognition of structure or method to obtain it may be mere wish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claim written description requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed genus may be supported by sufficient description of a representative number of species by actual reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure/physical properties or functional characteristics coupled with a known/disclosed correlation) sufficient to show inventor was in possession of the claimed genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Eli Lilly; Juno Therapeutics: specification must lead skilled artisan to understand inventor possessed entire claimed scope; Ariad purpose: prevent claims from overreaching disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative number of species must reflect genus variation
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'representative number of species' means the species adequately described are representative of the entire genus; when substantial variation exists, a sufficient variety of species must be described to reflect that variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AbbVie: disclosing only one structurally similar species may not be representative. Conversely, in some circumstances one species may support a genus if disclosure indicates invention of species sufficient to constitute the genus (Enzo Biochem; Rasmussen; In re Herschler). Consider whether disclosure provides blaze marks or other means to identify which species would possess claimed attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification cannot always support expansive claim language from one embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification that clearly describes one embodiment does not necessarily support broad/generic claim language unless skilled artisan would understand inventor possessed the broader claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LizardTech: disclose only particular method may not support generic claims; Tronzo: species in parent may not support genus in child when specification taught against other species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner initial burden and applicant responsibility for amended/new claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasoning why persons skilled in the art would not recognize in the original disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims; when filing an amendment an applicant should show support in the original disclosure for new or amended claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Wertheim; MPEP §§714.02 and 2163.06: applicant should specifically point out support for amendments. Cases: Hyatt v. Boone; In re Wright; In re Robins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each claim limitation must be supported in originally filed disclosure for priority/benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with written description or to be entitled to an earlier priority/filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119/120/365/386, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If explicit limitation is not present, show that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at filing that the description requires that limitation. Inherency must be proven clearly, not by possibilities. Cases: In re Robertson; Kennecott; Yeda Research; Regents of Univ. of Minnesota v. Gilead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must include all elements described as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must include all elements which applicant has described as essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an element described as essential is not claimed, new/amended claims lacking such support must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or priority/benefit denied. Cases: Johnson Worldwide; Gentry Gallery; Tronzo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences when disclosure lacks support for claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the originally filed disclosure does not provide support for each claim limitation, or if an element described as essential is not claimed, a new or amended claim must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (lack of adequate written description), or priority/benefit must be denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this when examiner or applicant cannot show express/implicit/inherent support; follow rejection protocols in Office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete patentability determination and clear communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must complete the patentability determination under all relevant statutory provisions (35 U.S.C. 101, 112, 102, 103) and clearly communicate findings, conclusions, and their bases in any Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review all proposed rejections and their bases before imposing any rejection; when possible, offer helpful suggestions on how to overcome rejections and ensure findings are clearly explained.
